title: Impact of COPS Grant on Violent Crime Rates

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy
Difference-in-differences (DID) is the appropriate method here. We compare the change in violent crime rates before and after COPS grant allocation between municipalities that received grants (treated) versus those that did not (control). The key assumption is parallel trends: in the absence of treatment, treated and control municipalities would have experienced similar trends in violent crime rates.

## 2. R Code
```r
# Load required libraries
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(lfe)
library(ggplot2)

# Read the data
data <- read_csv("experiments/exp_b/data/s46_data.csv")

# Basic summary statistics
print("Data Summary:")
print(summary(data))

# Check treatment assignment
print("\nTreatment Assignment:")
treatment_table <- data %>% 
  group_by(treated) %>% 
  summarise(n_units = n_distinct(unit_id), .groups = 'drop')
print(treatment_table)

# Main DID regression with unit and time fixed effects
did_model <- felm(y ~ treat_x_post | unit_id + period | 0 | unit_id, data = data)

print("\n=== MAIN DID RESULTS ===")
print(summary(did_model))

# Extract and print the key coefficient
did_coefficient <- coef(did_model)["treat_x_post"]
did_se <- summary(did_model)$coefficients["treat_x_post", "Std. Error"]
did_pvalue <- summary(did_model)$coefficients["treat_x_post", "Pr(>|t|)"]

print(paste("\nDID Coefficient:", round(did_coefficient, 4)))
print(paste("Standard Error:", round(did_se, 4)))
print(paste("P-value:", round(did_pvalue, 4)))

# Convert to percentage change interpretation
percent_change <- (exp(did_coefficient) - 1) * 100
print(paste("Implied percentage change in violent crime rate:", round(percent_change, 2), "%"))

# Robustness Check 1: Parallel trends test (if multiple pre-periods available)
print("\n=== ROBUSTNESS CHECKS ===")

# Check number of periods
periods_summary <- data %>% 
  group_by(post) %>% 
  summarise(n_periods = n_distinct(period), .groups = 'drop')
print("Periods summary:")
print(periods_summary)

# Robustness Check 2: Simple DID without fixed effects (for comparison)
simple_did <- lm(y ~ treated + post + treat_x_post, data = data)
print("\nSimple DID (without fixed effects):")
print(summary(simple_did)$coefficients["treat_x_post", ])

# Robustness Check 3: Check pre-treatment trends if multiple pre-periods exist
pre_treatment <- data %>% filter(post == 0)
if(length(unique(pre_treatment$period)) > 1) {
  trend_test <- lm(y ~ treated * period, data = pre_treatment)
  interaction_coef <- coef(trend_test)["treated:period"]
  interaction_pval <- summary(trend_test)$coefficients["treated:period", "Pr(>|t|)"]
  print(paste("\nPre-treatment trend difference (treated vs control):", round(interaction_coef, 4)))
  print(paste("P-value for trend difference:", round(interaction_pval, 4)))
}

# Plot average outcomes by treatment status and time
plot_data <- data %>%
  group_by(treated, post) %>%
  summarise(mean_y = mean(y, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = 'drop') %>%
  mutate(group = ifelse(treated == 1, "Treated", "Control"),
         time = ifelse(post == 1, "Post", "Pre"))

print("\nMean outcomes by group and period:")
print(plot_data)

# Create a simple visualization
ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = time, y = mean_y, color = group, group = group)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(title = "COPS Grant Impact on Log Violent Crime Rate",
       x = "Period", y = "Mean Log Violent Crime Rate",
       color = "Group") +
  theme_minimal()

# Final result summary
print("\n=== FINAL RESULTS SUMMARY ===")
print(paste("COPS Grant Effect on Log Violent Crime Rate:", round(did_coefficient, 4)))
print(paste("95% Confidence Interval: [", 
            round(did_coefficient - 1.96*did_se, 4), ",", 
            round(did_coefficient + 1.96*did_se, 4), "]"))
print(paste("Statistical Significance:", ifelse(did_pvalue < 0.05, "Significant", "Not Significant")))
```

## 3. Expected Findings
I expect a negative coefficient (around -0.1 to -0.3), indicating that COPS grants reduce violent crime rates by approximately 10-25%. This is consistent with economic theory that increased police presence deters crime through enhanced law enforcement capacity and visibility. The magnitude should be meaningful but not extreme, as police hiring is one of many factors affecting crime rates, and there may be implementation lags in the effectiveness of newly hired officers.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Compare changes in violent crime rates between municipalities that received the grant and those that did not, before and after the grant allocation.
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: The analysis reveals a positive effect of the COPS grant on the violent crime rate.
